parts.note: a Pole is a native of Poland, one European
cat is old jazz slang for a hip enthusiast

explanation.surface: Someone named Fitch is introduced as a Continental lover of jazz.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fitch' reads as a surname, but it is the old name for the European polecat and its fur.
explanation.definitionFit: Fitch is an old name for the European polecat, a weasel-like mammal.

parts.note: not formal wear in a sombre colour but an outfit for the dark, worn at night in bed

explanation.surface: A sober, dark-coloured business suit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dark' suggests colour, but it means night-time.
explanation.definitionFit: Nightwear consisting of loose jacket and trousers is the suit worn in bed after dark.

clue.text: Short of a platform? I call you first in a spiritless way

parts.note: to lack something is to be short of it
a dais is a raised platform
taken as written

indicators.note: first means only the opening letter of you is used

explanation.surface: Someone lacking a stage calls you up first, but without any enthusiasm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' takes Y from 'you', which ends the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To act listlessly or without energy is to behave in a lazy, unenthusiastic manner.

clue.text: Some pork for composer dropping in

indicators.note: dropping means the letters of the following little word fall out of the composer's name

parts.note: Chopin was a Polish composer
taken as written

explanation.surface: A composer pops in for some pork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping' removes IN from CHOPIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A pork chop is a cut of meat from the pig.

parts.note: taken as written
an aster is a daisy-like flower

explanation.surface: A poem titled To Daisy, as Robert Browning might have written it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Browning' suggests the poet Robert Browning; the answer is a kitchen appliance that browns bread. The Browning Version is also a Rattigan play.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchen appliance whose job is to brown bread slices.

clue.text: Abernethy, for example, fired but not finished

explanation.surface: Something called Abernethy has been fired before it was completed.
explanation.walkthrough: An Abernethy is a plain Scottish biscuit flavoured with caraway. In pottery, biscuit is ware fired once but not yet glazed.
explanation.definitionFit: An Abernethy is a kind of plain biscuit; potters call once-fired, unglazed clay ware biscuit.

parts.note: not a sports fixture but a long cushion supporting two heads on a double bed

explanation.surface: A support for a baseball double-header or two-headed creature.
explanation.walkthrough: A double-header sounds like a sporting fixture; here it is a double bed holding two heads, propped by one long pillow.
explanation.definitionFit: A long, firm pillow that runs across a double bed, supporting both sleepers' heads.

indicators.note: to scupper is to wreck, so the trick's letters are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A trick is bound to be foiled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scupper' rearranges RUSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sure means being confident or in no doubt.

indicators.note: change tells you to alter the order of the letters of the station phrase

explanation.surface: Is the seat booked? Passengers change trains at the end of the line in Devon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' rearranges ATDEVONTERMINUS; 'Reserved' looks like a booked seat but means emotionally restrained.
explanation.definitionFit: A reserved person keeps feelings hidden, rarely showing affection or emotion openly.

clue.text: This silk sets our constituents off

indicators.note: the component letters of the two words are set off in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A silk that shows off the elected people who make up our electorate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'constituents off' rearranges SETSOUR. Tussore is a coarse wild silk from India.
explanation.definitionFit: Tussore is a coarse, golden-brown wild silk from Indian silkworms.

parts.note: a jack is a flag, and a college teaching every craft would be one of all trades, so its flag names a handy person

explanation.surface: A banner hoisted above a polytechnic.
explanation.walkthrough: The jack is a ship's flag; a college of all trades would fly its own jack, giving the phrase for someone handy at everything.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a versatile handyman, skilled at many kinds of work.

parts.note: to swallow is to eat

explanation.surface: Something for a male bird of the swallow kind to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swallow' looks like the bird, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Flesh of animals is a staple foodstuff.

clue.text: Virginia is one in this condition

explanation.surface: Virginia is said to be in this particular condition.
explanation.walkthrough: Virginia is one of the United States; a state is also a condition, as in a state of shock.
explanation.definitionFit: Virginia is a US political unit of that kind; the word also means a condition or situation.

parts.note: MM is the Military Medal, a British gallantry award
O looks like a ring

explanation.surface: A medal on a ring, ready to be fired.
explanation.walkthrough: MM is the Military Medal, a British decoration for bravery.
explanation.definitionFit: Ammunition is what a gun fires, hence something for firing.

explanation.surface: A query about fast motor boats.
explanation.walkthrough: Fleet as an adjective means swift; a fleet is a group of ships.
explanation.definitionFit: Swift-footed means quick; a navy's group of ships is also called this.

indicators.note: has says the word that follows contains the answer, and done says the run of its letters is complete at its front

explanation.surface: An employee called Frank has worked extra hours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has done' marks the answer as the opening run of 'overtime'; read another way, OVER (done) plus T (time). 'Frank' looks like a name but is the adjective meaning open.
explanation.definitionFit: Overt means open and unconcealed, as a frank remark is.

clue.text: But it will not secure loose plaster

definitions.text: But it will not secure loose plaster

indicators.note: loose says the letters of plaster are set free to fall into a new order

explanation.surface: A warning that a certain office gadget is useless for fixing crumbling plaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loose' rearranges PLASTER; the whole clue also describes the office tool, which fastens paper but not plaster.
explanation.definitionFit: A desk device that fastens papers with wire clips cannot hold up crumbling wall plaster.

indicators.note: about means the word for regret goes round the word for flat

parts.note: to rue is to regret
flat and even both mean level

explanation.surface: Someone regrets what the flat has earned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flat' looks like an apartment, but it means level; 'about' signals the regret word going round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Revenue is income or takings, the money a business brings in.

indicators.note: endlessly says the word for lad loses its last letter

parts.note: a lad is a boy
swell is old slang for a dandy, and as an adjective means stylish

explanation.surface: A biographer's son is forever dandified.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' cuts the Y from BOY to give BO. James Boswell wrote the Life of Samuel Johnson.
explanation.definitionFit: James Boswell wrote the famous Life of Samuel Johnson, the model of English life-writing.

parts.note: someone in a room of books who dips into them casually rather than studying

explanation.surface: Someone in the reading room who isn't taking it seriously.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 is LIBRARY; the person meant only leafs through the shelves.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who leafs casually through books rather than studying them.

parts.note: Libra, the zodiac sign, is the scales

explanation.surface: A Reading model railway built to scale needs space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reading' looks like the Berkshire town on the railway, but it is reading books.
explanation.definitionFit: A room where books are kept and read.

clue.text: Dog approaching a hill needs a keeper

parts.note: a cur is a mongrel dog
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A dog heading for a hill needs someone to look after it.
explanation.walkthrough: TOR is a rocky hilltop, common in the names of English moorland hills.
explanation.definitionFit: A curator is the custodian in charge of a museum or collection.

clue.text: Care needed in auction, when item three comes first

indicators.note: the third letter of auction is moved up to stand at the start

explanation.surface: Bidders are warned to be careful when lot three is sold first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'item three comes first' moves the third letter, C, of AUCTION to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Caution means carefulness, taking care to avoid danger.

explanation.surface: Audience numbers for sailors.
explanation.walkthrough: Ratings are TV audience figures; ratings are also non-commissioned sailors in the Royal Navy.
explanation.definitionFit: Measures of television audience size; also ordinary seamen of no officer rank.

clue.text: Old buckle causes cry of pain

explanation.surface: An antique buckle makes someone yelp.
explanation.walkthrough: An ouch is an archaic word for a clasp or brooch; it is also the exclamation of pain.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic word meant a jewelled clasp or brooch; it is also what people shout when hurt.

clue.text: Dealing with U-boat that is damaged

indicators.note: damaged says the letters of the submarine's name are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: Coping with a submarine that has been hit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'damaged' rearranges UBOAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A book about whales is one concerning or dealing with them.

explanation.surface: A shoemaker required something in order to keep going.
explanation.walkthrough: A cordwainer is a shoemaker, who shapes shoes on a foot-shaped block called a last; to last is to endure.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoemaker's wooden foot model is called this; the verb also means to persist or go on.

clue.text: A ringer for one of the "Brontes"

explanation.surface: A lookalike for one of the Brontë sisters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ringer' suggests a double, but it is something that rings. The Brontës published as Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell.
explanation.definitionFit: A church chime rings; the Brontë sisters published under the pen-name surname of Currer, Ellis and Acton.

explanation.surface: A dramatic colony of actors.
explanation.walkthrough: Camp means exaggerated and theatrical; a camp is also a temporary settlement.
explanation.definitionFit: Camp describes flamboyant, over-the-top style; it also means a group of tents or huts.

clue.text: Only I can pass in it

definitions.text: Only I can pass in it

parts.words: Only I can pass in it
parts.note: a test where the only examiner and the only candidate are the same person, so nobody else can pass

explanation.surface: Boasting about a test nobody else can get through.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'it' reads as an ordinary exam; the twist is that the one being tested is also the examiner.
explanation.definitionFit: Introspection means scrutinising your own conduct, a test where you set and sit the paper.

clue.text: Payment to author from queen's office

explanation.surface: An author's fee comes out of a monarch's department.
explanation.walkthrough: A royalty is a writer's share of sales; royalty is also the rank or office of a king or queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Writers receive a percentage fee on each copy sold; the word also means regal status.

clue.text: Kids who make us feel the pinch

definitions.text: who make us feel the pinch

explanation.surface: Children who leave their parents short of money.
explanation.walkthrough: Nippers are small children in British slang; nippers are also pincers, tools that pinch.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for small children; also pincers or claws that grip and squeeze.
